solutions.check: 32 entries verified against the grid (lengths, crossings, linked-clue mapping)

clue.text: Who'd love to make you smart?

definitions.text: Who'd love to make you smart?

blocks.note: the surface offers a well-meaning teacher, somebody keen to do you good
smart is also the verb that means to sting, so what is on offer is pain rather than cleverness

explanation.surface: Someone is held out as the person eager to sharpen your wits.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Smart' is an adjective in the surface, meaning clever, and a verb in the answer, meaning to sting. 'Love to' is the giveaway, because only one sort of person enjoys causing that.
explanation.definitionFit: A sadist takes pleasure in inflicting pain, and a blow that makes you smart is exactly the pain meant.

clue.text: Politician in hasty arrangement has 'end of party' feeling

indicators.note: a politician put in something is surrounded by it, with the other letters closing on either side
an arrangement is however you choose to set the pieces out, so the letters need not stay as given
the end of a word is the letter it finishes on

blocks.note: the five letters of HASTY reset
mp = member of parliament, the crossword's standard politician
the last letter of partY

explanation.surface: A politician caught up in a rushed arrangement is left flat once the party is over.
explanation.walkthrough: The quotation marks around 'end of party' dress it up as a mood when it is an instruction to take one letter. 'Feeling' stands alone at the end and is the whole definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Sympathy is fellow feeling, the sharing of what someone else is going through, so the bare noun covers it.

clue.text: Confronted over drink that's less stimulating

indicators.note: something turned over shows the same letters back to front

blocks.note: to face someone is to confront them, and FACED is set down here from its last letter back to its first

explanation.surface: An accusation made over a cup of something milder than usual.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Over' poses as the preposition that always follows 'confronted' and is the instruction to read backwards. Everything after it is definition, right to the end of the clue.
explanation.definitionFit: Decaf is coffee with the caffeine taken out, the same drink without the kick that keeps you awake.

clue.text: Castrati put out about Latin bloke who scored

indicators.note: to be put out is to be thrown out of order, and letters thrown out of order can be reset any way
one thing placed about another is wrapped round it, so the outer letters split to make room

blocks.note: the eight letters of CASTRATI redealt
l = latin, the dictionary's tag for the language

explanation.surface: Castrato singers are indignant about a Latin gentleman's conquests.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Scored' is the footballer's or the seducer's verb in the surface and the composer's in the answer. Domenico Scarlatti wrote over five hundred keyboard sonatas, and castrati sang in his lifetime, which is why the fodder sits so quietly.
explanation.definitionFit: Scarlatti wrote musical scores for a living, so the man who scored is the composer rather than the goalscorer.

clue.text: Act a bit odd on having a roll?

indicators.note: something odd is not as it should be, and letters not as they should be have been moved about

blocks.note: seven of the eight letters, straight off the page
the article supplies the eighth letter

explanation.surface: Somebody is behaving strangely because they are having a roll.
explanation.walkthrough: Only 'roll' is the definition; the 'a' in front of it belongs to the letters being shuffled. Cyclops leaves 'having a roll' sitting there to be read as the bedroom idiom.
explanation.definitionFit: A ciabatta is the flat, floury Italian loaf, sold roll-sized in every British sandwich shop.

clue.text: One with special knowledge of cool drink, it's said

indicators.note: what is said arrives as sound, and the ear cannot tell which spelling produced it

blocks.note: cool in the fashionable sense is IN and the drink is CIDER; spoken as one word they are the answer

explanation.surface: Someone who knows more than they should about a chilled drink.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cool' is the 1960s sense, fashionable rather than cold, which is why the drink has to be cider and not something iced. The join between the two spoken words is where the S appears.
explanation.definitionFit: An insider is someone within an organisation who knows what outsiders do not, which is special knowledge by position.

clue.text: PC language, so coarse cabbies be gone!

indicators.note: coarse work is rough and unfinished, and letters left rough sit in no fixed order
what is gone has left the word it was in, taking its letters out of the count

blocks.note: cabbies are taxi drivers, and the word is the raw material
the B and E that walk out, dropping CABBIES to the five letters CABIS

explanation.surface: A rant demanding that coarse cab drivers clear off.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Be gone!' is an order in the surface and two jobs in the parse, the word naming its own letters and the command sending them away. 'PC' is the computer here, not the constable or the correctness.
explanation.definitionFit: BASIC is the beginner's programming language that came built into early home computers, so a PC speaks it.

clue.text: Pissed guy? Walk with care on this

definitions.note: The definition points at the answer rather than naming it, 'this' standing in for the noun, which is how a phrase about walking can define a thing.

blocks.note: tight is British slang for drunk, as in 'tight as a tick'
a guy is the line that steadies a tent or a mast

explanation.surface: A drunk man is warned to watch his step.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pissed guy' looks like one phrase for one person and is two words for two pieces. A guy rope is the cord that holds a tent down, so 'guy' on its own can be the rope.
explanation.definitionFit: A tightrope is the wire an acrobat crosses, and nothing else asks for such care underfoot.

clue.text: Bloody channel's 'creative' appropriation of old monarch!

indicators.note: to appropriate a thing is to take it into your own keeping, and what is taken in sits inside

blocks.note: arty is what the scare quotes mean: creative, or claiming to be
er = Elizabeth Regina, the late queen's cipher and the crossword's standard monarch

explanation.surface: A television channel is accused of helping itself to a dead monarch in the name of art.
explanation.walkthrough: The scare quotes on 'creative' are a dig at television costume drama and also the whole of that piece. 'Bloody' is swearing in the surface and anatomy in the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: An artery is a vessel carrying blood away from the heart, so it is a channel with blood in it quite literally.

clue.text: Foreign minister's a scurrilous comic that is on right

indicators.note: in a down entry one thing sits on another by being written above it, so the piece named first takes the higher squares

blocks.note: Viz is the filthy British comic magazine, founded in Newcastle in 1979
ie is the Latin id est, which is English 'that is'
r = right, the map and stage-direction abbreviation

explanation.surface: A foreign minister turns out to be a scandalous joke with right-wing leanings.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Comic' is the magazine rather than the stand-up, and Viz trades in exactly the scurrility the surface pins on the minister. A vizier serves a Muslim ruler, so 'foreign' is pulling its weight.
explanation.definitionFit: A vizier is a high minister of state in a Muslim country, most familiarly the grand vizier of the Ottoman court.

clue.text: "Cover for dogs" ludicrously portrayed in Comic Sans

indicators.note: to portray a thing ludicrously is to set it down in a ridiculous shape, and the letters take a shape of their own

blocks.note: the nine letters of the typeface everybody mocks

explanation.surface: A sign reading 'Cover for dogs', absurdly set in the world's most ridiculed typeface.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dogs' is British slang for feet, so the cover wanted is footwear rather than anything a kennel sells. Comic Sans is the typeface designers love to hate, which is what earns it 'ludicrously'.
explanation.definitionFit: Moccasins are soft leather shoes, and 'dogs' has meant feet in British slang for a century.

clue.text: see 12ac.
(& 11ac.) Waving US flag with horror

indicators.note: a flag being waved never holds still, and letters that will not hold still can land in any order

blocks.note: the ten letters, the little word 'with' included

explanation.surface: Somebody watches the Stars and Stripes being waved and is appalled.
explanation.walkthrough: 'With horror' reads as one phrase about the watcher, yet 'with' hands over four of the letters and 'horror' alone is the definition. The answer runs across two entries, 12 then 11.
explanation.definitionFit: An awful sight is something you flinch from looking at, which is what a horror is.

clue.text: Some finger pointing – tad ironic maybe

definitions.note: The answer is the thing that does the pointing rather than the act of it; a car's indicator began life as a semaphore arm that flicked out like a finger.

indicators.note: what is only maybe so need not be exactly as written, and letters that need not stay as written can be reordered

blocks.note: the nine letters waiting to be reset

explanation.surface: A certain amount of blame is being thrown about, which is slightly ironic.
explanation.walkthrough: The dash invites you to read the second half as a comment on the first, when it is the raw material. The trafficator on a pre-war car really was a little arm that flicked out to point.
explanation.definitionFit: An indicator is whatever points the way, a flashing arm or a gauge's needle, and pointing a finger is the same gesture.

clue.text: Poor luvvie needs rest badly, pet

indicators.note: a thing done badly comes out wrong, and letters put down wrong are in the wrong order

blocks.note: a ham is an actor who overdoes it, and luvvie is the British press's word for a theatrical
the four letters of REST redealt

explanation.surface: A washed-up actor badly needs a break, poor thing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rest' is the actor's word for being out of work as well as four letters, and 'poor' does duty as both pity and a verdict on the acting. The definition is the single word after the comma.
explanation.definitionFit: A hamster is the small caged rodent children keep, so 'pet' names it by the class it belongs to.

clue.text: You might claim booze is from Iceland – I'm dubious

definitions.note: The definition is the sentence the answer completes rather than a synonym for it: what you might claim the booze is, is medicinal.

indicators.note: what is dubious cannot be trusted to be what it says, and letters not to be trusted have shifted

blocks.note: the seven letters of ICELAND with I'M adding two more

explanation.surface: Somebody doubts the claim that the drink came from Iceland.
explanation.walkthrough: Iceland is a British frozen-food supermarket as well as a country, which is what makes buying booze there sound ordinary. 'I'm dubious' plays as the speaker's aside and gives up two of its letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Medicinal is what a drinker calls the brandy when they want it to sound prescribed rather than merely wanted.

clue.text: Front page right to reveal minister?

blocks.note: the recto is the front of a leaf, the right-hand page of an open book
r = right

explanation.surface: A newspaper's front page exposes a government minister.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Minister' is the churchman, not the cabinet member a front page would be chasing. Recto is the printer's name for the right-hand page, which is why the clue can ask for 'right' twice over.
explanation.definitionFit: A rector is the priest in charge of a Church of England parish, so 'minister' covers him by rank.

clue.text: Wow! Green-embracing Jeremy? Not quite

indicators.note: to embrace something is to get your arms right round it, so the embracing word closes on both sides
not quite the whole word means stopping one letter short of the end

blocks.note: Jeremy Corbyn, the Labour MP and former party leader, docked of his final N
lime is the sharp yellow-green

explanation.surface: An astonished cry at Jeremy Corbyn getting close to the Greens.
explanation.walkthrough: It is Corbyn's surname that is wanted, not his politics, and 'Green' is a colour rather than a party. 'Cor blimey' is Cockney for 'God blind me', worn down over a century into plain astonishment.
explanation.definitionFit: 'Cor blimey' is the London cry of amazement, the everyday British equivalent of 'Wow!'

clue.text: It's between Starmer and Trump mainly

definitions.text: It's between Starmer and Trump mainly

blocks.note: the surface is the state of the special relationship, something coming between a British prime minister and an American president
the main is an old word for the open sea, so this says the thing between them is water

explanation.surface: Whatever it is that stands between the British prime minister and the American president.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mainly' looks like the hedge every political sentence carries and is the clue's only cryptic signal, the main being the high sea. Keir Starmer is Britain's prime minister, so the two men stand on opposite shores.
explanation.definitionFit: The Atlantic is the ocean dividing Britain from the United States, which is literally what lies between the two leaders.

clue.text: Party about to get on course? A bit unusual

indicators.note: a party turned about faces the other way, and its letters are read back

blocks.note: a party is a do, and DO turned about reads OD
a course at dinner is a dish

explanation.surface: A political party looks about to get itself back on track.
explanation.walkthrough: 'On course' is the phrase the surface wants, a party correcting itself, and 'course' is really on its own as one of dinner's. The definition is the three words after the question mark.
explanation.definitionFit: Oddish is odd but only mildly so, which is the hedge that 'a bit unusual' makes.

clue.text: Pageboy's somewhat coquettish air? Cute

indicators.note: somewhat of a phrase is a part of it, and the part wanted is a run of letters lying unbroken inside

blocks.note: coquettisH AIR CUTe holds the seven letters in order once the spaces are ignored

explanation.surface: A pageboy is credited with a rather flirtatious, cute air.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark and the capital on 'Cute' are there to break the run up, and the letters cross three words and a piece of punctuation. A pageboy is a hairstyle as well as a boy in livery.
explanation.definitionFit: The pageboy is the chin-length bob with the ends rolled under, named for the hair of a medieval page.

clue.text: More than enough froth before initially empty sex

indicators.note: what comes before the rest is written in front of it, so this piece takes the opening squares
initially points at the initial of the word beside it, the letter it starts with

blocks.note: surf is the white froth the sea makes on the shore
the first letter of Empty
it = sex, the coy usage Elinor Glyn made famous as sex appeal

explanation.surface: A great deal of froth ahead of some hollow, unsatisfying sex.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Initially empty' is one phrase doing two jobs: 'initially' asks for a first letter and 'empty' is the word it comes from. 'It' for sex is among the oldest euphemisms the crossword keeps alive.
explanation.definitionFit: A surfeit is an excess, more of something than anyone needed, which is 'more than enough' exactly.

clue.text: Trump payee is raging

definitions.note: The first definition names a person rather than defining an adjective; Stormy is the working first name of the woman Trump's lawyer paid.

blocks.note: the adult-film actress paid $130,000 in hush money shortly before the 2016 election, known by her working first name
a sea or a night that rages is described by this adjective

explanation.surface: The person Trump wrote a cheque to is furious.
explanation.walkthrough: The two halves want different parts of speech, a name and an adjective, and 'is' hides the seam between them. That payment is what later became Trump's New York conviction.
explanation.definitionFit: Stormy is the first name of the woman Trump's lawyer paid off, and weather that rages is stormy weather.

clue.text: MI Five's head taken in, then put out

indicators.note: the head of a word is the letter at its front

blocks.note: lifted from the page as it stands; MI5 is Britain's domestic security service
the head of Five
someone taken in and given a meal has been fed

explanation.surface: The head of MI5 is taken in for questioning and then thrown out.
explanation.walkthrough: 'MI Five' is spelt out in words so that its first half can be lifted whole and its second cut to an initial. 'Taken in' is deception in the surface and dinner in the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: To be put out is to be annoyed or offended, which is the mild huffiness of being miffed.

clue.text: Apparently not yourself, pissed, noticing nothing

indicators.note: someone pissed cannot walk a straight line, and letters in that state keep no order either

blocks.note: the eight letters to be redealt
o = nothing, the zero on the page

explanation.surface: Somebody drunk enough to be unrecognisable, and noticing nothing at all.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Not yourself' reads as the usual excuse for odd behaviour and means wearing another identity altogether. 'Pissed' is drunkenness in the surface and an instruction in the parse.
explanation.definitionFit: To travel incognito is to go about under a false name, so you appear to be somebody other than yourself.

clue.text: (& 26ac.) Moving bloke with electronic implant doesn't cost much

definitions.note: The answer is the market-stall phrase said of a thing on sale, so it stands where a verb phrase stands: what is going cheap doesn't cost much.

indicators.note: something implanted is set inside the body it goes into, with that body closing over it

blocks.note: what is moving is going
a chap is a bloke
e = electronic, as in e-mail

explanation.surface: A man on the move with an electronic implant is not expensive to run.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Moving' is what a price does as much as a body, the auctioneer's 'going, going, gone'. The implant is a single letter, dropped into the middle of the bloke.
explanation.definitionFit: Something going cheap is on offer at a knock-down price, which is the market trader's way of saying it costs little.

clue.text: Some really crap sporty wear

indicators.note: some of a phrase is a part of it, and the part meant is a run of letters sitting unbroken inside

blocks.note: the run begins on the second L of 'really' and carries on into 'crap', stopping before the P

explanation.surface: A dismissive verdict on some genuinely terrible sportswear.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Some' is doing the hiding, and the run needs the second L of 'really' rather than the first. Lycra is the British trade name for the stretch fabric sold elsewhere as spandex.
explanation.definitionFit: Lycra is the stretch fabric that leggings and cycling shorts are made of, so it is what sporty clothing is.

clue.text: see 24ac.
Soldier after amusing, cheesy additions

indicators.note: in an across entry what comes after something is written to its right, so this piece takes the later squares

blocks.note: something amusing is fun
gi = an American private soldier, from 'government issue'

explanation.surface: A soldier arrives once the comedy is over, bringing cheesy extras with him.
explanation.walkthrough: The comma after 'amusing' hides the join: 'after' belongs to the wordplay and everything past it is definition. Mould is a fungus, which is what puts fungi into cheese.
explanation.definitionFit: The moulds that ripen a cheese and bloom on its rind are fungi, put there on purpose by the cheesemaker.

clue.text: Rather cheesy, this MP getting cuddled by whip

definitions.note: The answer is a cheese and the definition describes it with an adjective, 'this' pointing at the thing being called cheesy.

indicators.note: to be cuddled is to be held with arms right round you, so the cuddling word closes on both sides

blocks.note: the cat, short for cat-o'-nine-tails, is the whip sailors were flogged with
an MP is a Member of Parliament, and Member is what the House calls one

explanation.surface: A backbencher gets an affectionate squeeze from the party whip, which is a bit corny.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Whip' is the party official in the surface and the flogging rope in the parse. 'Member' is the MP's own title, which is how two letters on the page become six in the grid.
explanation.definitionFit: Camembert is the soft Normandy cheese sold in a round wooden box, so 'rather cheesy' is true of it in the most literal way.

clue.text: Representative of broadcast food shop scandal?

indicators.note: what is broadcast goes out as sound, and sound carries no spelling with it

blocks.note: a deli is the food shop and -gate has meant a scandal ever since Watergate; said one after the other they are the answer

explanation.surface: Someone held up as typical of a much-reported scandal at a food shop.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Broadcast' is the radio sense, not the scattering one that would make this an anagram. The -gate ending has meant a scandal since Watergate brought Nixon down in 1974.
explanation.definitionFit: A delegate is the person sent to speak for a group at a conference, a representative in the plainest sense.

clue.text: Rather short-sighted, unusually coy PM guards independence

indicators.note: what is unusual is not in its normal state, and letters out of their normal state are out of their normal order
a guard stands round whatever it protects, so these letters close on both sides of the one being guarded

blocks.note: the three letters of COY and the two of PM redealt
i = independence

explanation.surface: A bashful prime minister is protecting the country's independence.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Coy PM' reads as a character sketch and is five letters for shuffling; PM is not standing in for anything, it is printed on the page. Myopia is literal short-sightedness before it is ever the political kind.
explanation.definitionFit: Myopic is the medical word for short-sighted, unable to focus on anything far off, and it carries the political sense too.
